I am 73 years old. My bones ache in the morning, and my wife and I are the only ones left to work this land. After fifty years of farming these 5 mu in Quzhou, I know every patch of soil. I cannot chase high-risk profits anymore—I need crops that give steady returns without breaking my back.

My wheat is already in the ground from last autumn. It covers 3 mu, the same land I will plant maize on after the June harvest. Wheat and maize are my backbone; the machines can harvest and plant them quickly, and I understand their needs like my own heartbeat. I will top-dress the wheat with urea at green-up and irrigate three times from the well—green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. Two sprays will take care of the aphids and rust that always come. I expect about 480 jin per mu, maybe 500 if the spring rain helps.

For summer maize, I will buy hybrid seed from the county supply store—Zhengdan or something similar. Time is tight after wheat harvest; I will not waste days ploughing. No-tillage seeding right behind the combine saves precious hours and keeps soil moisture. One round of pesticide at the seedling stage should be enough, and I will irrigate twice when the weather turns dry in July and August. I hope for 520 jin per mu.

I still keep 2 mu of cotton out of habit and because the price was acceptable last year. But cotton is cruel to old hands—picking season exhausts us. I use improved Bt cotton seed to reduce bollworm spraying, though I still need four pesticide applications for other pests. I will rotary-till the cotton plot in early spring, lay down compound fertilizer, and irrigate three times during flowering and boll-setting. I hope for 95 jin of lint per mu, but if my wife's knees act up during picking, we might hire help.

I keep fertilizer moderate. Too much nitrogen wastes money and makes wheat lodge. My well gives water, but pumping costs electricity, so I irrigate only when the crops truly thirst. At my age, I do not gamble on new methods—I do what has fed my family for fifty years.
